title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Respiratory System
path: Anatomy and Physiology of the Respiratory System

headings.title: Introduction to the Respiratory System
headings.content: The respiratory system is a vital biological network responsible for supplying oxygen to the body tissues and removing carbon dioxide, a metabolic waste product. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice in Nigeria, mastering this system is essential for recognizing respiratory distress, managing airway patency, and understanding acid-base balance. The respiratory process is broadly divided into two main physiological functions: external respiration, which involves the exchange of gases between the atmosphere and the blood within the lungs, and internal respiration, which is the exchange of gases between the circulating blood and the body's peripheral tissues. Additionally, the respiratory system plays a crucial role in non-respiratory functions such as pH regulation of the blood, vocalization through the larynx, olfaction via the nasal cavity, and defending the body against inhaled pathogens through protective mechanisms like coughing, sneezing, and mucociliary clearance. Anatomically, the respiratory tract is systematically categorized into the upper and lower respiratory tracts, each possessing specialized structures designed to filter, warm, and humidify inspired air before it reaches the delicate gas-exchange surfaces in the lungs. Understanding these foundational concepts allows nursing professionals to anticipate complications in patients with respiratory pathologies, implement appropriate interventions, and monitor oxygenation status effectively across diverse healthcare settings.

headings.title: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
headings.content: The upper respiratory tract consists of structures located outside the thoracic cavity, primarily including the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and the pharynx. The nose and nasal cavity are lined with a highly vascular mucous membrane and ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium. As air enters through the nares, it is warmed by the rich capillary network, humidified by moisture from mucous secretions, and filtered of large particulate matter by coarse hairs known as vibrissae. The paranasal sinuses—frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid, and maxillary—act as resonating chambers for speech and help lighten the skull bones, while also producing mucus that drains into the nasal cavity. The pharynx, or throat, serves as a muscular funnel-shaped passageway shared by both the respiratory and digestive systems. It is anatomically subdivided into three regions: the nasopharynx, which serves strictly as an airway and houses the pharyngeal tonsils; the oropharynx, a common passage for food and air containing the palatine and lingual tonsils; and the laryngopharynx, which extends down to the larynx and esophagus. Nursing assessments of the upper airway are critical for identifying obstructions, evaluating the patency of air passages, and managing patients with upper respiratory infections or trauma. Recognizing the structural continuity and protective mucous linings of these upper structures helps nurses understand how localized infections can easily spread downward into the lower respiratory tree.

headings.title: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
headings.content: The lower respiratory tract begins inferior to the larynx and is entirely contained within the thoracic cavity, comprising the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and the lungs. The larynx, often referred to as the voice box, guards the entrance to the lower respiratory tract and contains the vocal cords alongside the epiglottis, a flexible cartilage flap that closes off the trachea during swallowing to prevent aspiration. Extending downward from the larynx is the trachea, a rigid tube supported by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that prevent its collapse during pressure changes. The trachea bifurcates at the carina into the right and left primary main bronchi, which enter the lungs at the hilum. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left, making it a common site for the lodgment of aspirated foreign objects—a vital clinical pearl for nursing assessment. Within the lung parenchyma, the primary bronchi branch repeatedly into secondary (lobar) bronchi, tertiary (segmental) bronchi, and progressively smaller bronchioles. Unlike the trachea and large bronchi, bronchioles lack cartilage support and rely instead on smooth muscle tone to regulate airway diameter, allowing for bronchodilation and bronchoconstriction under autonomic nervous system control. The entire lower respiratory tract is lined with ciliated epithelium and mucus-producing goblet cells, forming the mucociliary escalator that constantly sweeps trapped dust, debris, and pathogens upward toward the pharynx where they can be swallowed or expectorated, protecting the deep lung tissue from infection.

headings.title: Microscopic Structure of the Lungs and Alveoli
headings.content: The microscopic architecture of the lungs is specifically engineered to maximize the surface area available for gas exchange. Terminal bronchioles subdivide into respiratory bronchioles, which then lead into alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and ultimately millions of microscopic air sacs known as alveoli. The walls of the alveoli are composed primarily of Type I alveolar cells, which are extremely thin simple squamous epithelial cells forming the structural basis of the alveolar wall. Interspersed among these are Type II alveolar cells, specialized cuboidal cells responsible for secreting pulmonary surfactant—a complex lipoprotein mixture that reduces surface tension within the fluid lining the alveoli, preventing them from collapsing at the end of expiration and decreasing the work of breathing. Additionally, alveolar macrophages (dust cells) patrol the internal surfaces, phagocytizing airborne pathogens, dust particles, and cellular debris that bypass the upper airway defenses. The actual exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occurs across the respiratory membrane, also known as the blood-air barrier. This ultra-thin barrier consists of the alveolar epithelium, its fused basement membrane, and the capillary endothelium. The immense total surface area of the millions of alveoli, combined with the extreme thinness of the respiratory membrane, allows for rapid, efficient diffusion of gases down their respective partial pressure gradients, ensuring adequate tissue oxygenation throughout the body.

headings.title: Mechanics of Pulmonary Ventilation
headings.content: Mechanics of pulmonary ventilation refer to the physical processes of air flowing into and out of the lungs, driven by pressure gradients established by changes in thoracic cavity volume. According to Boyle's Law, pressure and volume of a gas are inversely related: as volume increases, pressure decreases, and vice versa. Inspiration is an active process initiated by the contraction of the primary inspiratory muscles—the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles. When the dome-shaped diaphragm contracts, it flattens and moves inferiorly, while the contraction of the external intercostals lifts the rib cage upward and outward. These coordinated movements expand the vertical and anteroposterior dimensions of the thoracic cavity. As the thoracic volume increases, the intrapleural pressure (pressure within the pleural cavity) drops, causing the lungs to expand along with the chest wall. Consequently, the intrapulmonary pressure (pressure inside the alveoli) falls below atmospheric pressure, creating a negative pressure gradient that draws air rapidly into the lungs until pressures equalize. Expiration during quiet breathing is normally a passive process relying on the elastic recoil of the lung tissue and relaxation of the inspiratory muscles, which decreases thoracic volume, raises intrapulmonary pressure above atmospheric pressure, and forces air out. Forced expiration, however, becomes an active process engaging internal intercostal muscles and abdominal wall muscles to rapidly depress the ribs and push abdominal organs upward against the diaphragm.

headings.title: Gas Exchange and Transport
headings.content: Gas exchange in the lungs and systemic tissues occurs passively via simple diffusion, driven by differences in partial pressures of gases. Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures states that the total pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is the sum of the pressures exerted by each individual gas. Gases diffuse from an area of higher partial pressure to an area of lower partial pressure. In the alveoli, oxygen has a high partial pressure, causing it to diffuse across the respiratory membrane into the deoxygenated pulmonary capillary blood, where oxygen partial pressure is lower. Conversely, carbon dioxide has a higher partial pressure in the incoming capillary blood than in the alveoli, causing it to diffuse into the alveolar space to be exhaled. Once in the blood, oxygen is transported primarily bound to hemoglobin within red blood cells as oxyhemoglobin (about 98.5%), with only a small fraction dissolved directly in the plasma. The affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen is influenced by factors such as blood pH, temperature, and carbon dioxide concentration—a phenomenon known as the Bohr effect, where increased acidity or carbon dioxide promotes oxygen release in metabolically active tissues. Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood via three main mechanisms: dissolved in plasma (about 7-10%), bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin (about 20%), and primarily transported as bicarbonate ions dissolved in plasma (about 70%), generated via the action of carbonic anhydrase within red blood cells, which plays a pivotal role in systemic acid-base balance.

headings.title: Neural and Chemical Regulation of Respiration
headings.content: Respiration is tightly regulated by neural centers in the brainstem to maintain homeostatic blood gas levels and pH, responding dynamically to the body's metabolic demands. The respiratory center is located within the medulla oblongata and pons. The medullary respiratory center contains the dorsal respiratory group (DRG), which controls the basic rhythm of breathing by stimulating the diaphragm and external intercostals, and the ventral respiratory group (VRG), which becomes active during forced breathing and drives accessory muscles for expiration and heavy inspiration. The pontine respiratory group (formerly known as the pneumotaxic and apneustic centers) fine-tunes the transition between inhalation and exhalation, ensuring smooth, coordinated breathing patterns. These neural centers receive constant sensory input from central and peripheral chemoreceptors. Central chemoreceptors, located on the ventral surface of the medulla, monitor the pH and carbon dioxide levels of the cerebrospinal fluid; an increase in hydrogen ions or carbon dioxide strongly stimulates ventilation. Peripheral chemoreceptors, situated in the carotid and aortic bodies, are sensitive to arterial blood levels of oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH, though they primarily drive increased ventilation when arterial oxygen levels drop precipitously (hypoxemia). Additionally, pulmonary irritant receptors and stretch receptors in the visceral pleura and bronchioles prevent lung overinflation via the Hering-Breuer reflex, protecting delicate lung tissues from barotrauma during deep inspiration.

headings.title: Clinical Implications for Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Clinical nursing assessment of the respiratory system requires a systematic approach encompassing history taking, physical examination, and interpretation of diagnostic data. Nurses must assess key indicators of respiratory distress, including respiratory rate, depth, rhythm, use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, and skin color changes such as central or peripheral cyanosis. Inspection includes evaluating chest symmetry and shape, noting conditions like barrel chest in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients. Palpation helps identify areas of tenderness, structural abnormalities, and tactile fremitus, while percussion detects underlying tissue density variations, differentiating hollow resonant sounds in healthy lung tissue from dull sounds indicative of consolidation or pleural effusion. Auscultation using a stethoscope is critical for listening to breath sounds across lung fields, distinguishing normal vesicular, bronchovesicular, and bronchial sounds from abnormal adventitious sounds such as crackles (rales), wheezes, rhonchi, and pleural friction rubs. Nurses also monitor oxygenation status continuously using pulse oximetry to measure peripheral oxygen saturation ($SpO_2$) and analyze arterial blood gas (ABG) reports to evaluate ventilation, oxygenation, and acid-base status. Recognizing these clinical findings early empowers nursing professionals in Nigeria and globally to initiate timely interventions, administer oxygen therapy safely, suction airways when indicated, and collaborate effectively with interprofessional healthcare teams to improve patient outcomes.
